results.headline: On tribal land where EPA is the regulator, 13.7-19.2% of health-based violations begun since 2015 are still unaddressed today. The state median is 1.7%. West Virginia is at 21.5% (482 open, 204K people), Louisiana has 710 open (456K people), and 514 community systems (1.59M people) have one open for 2+ years.
results.checked: I deduped to one row per violation (PWSID + VIOLATION_ID), since each violation repeats once per enforcement action. I kept health-based violations only (IS_HEALTH_BASED_IND='Y') that began 2015-01-01 or later. For each one I counted formal, informal and resolving actions and read its status today, then joined the water-systems table for regulator, type and population. Code 5200 is split out: it reads as the lead-pipe inventory rule, with every top-list row starting 2024-10-17. Finally I compared regulators to each other and pulled the list of violations open 2+ years.
results.hit_means: The regulator, not the water, decides whether a violation gets closed. A 10x gap to the state median on tribal land points at EPA's own backlog. WV and LA are the state outliers, with named systems attached.
results.miss_means: If the tribal, WV and LA rates had sat near the 1.7% state median, the gap would be noise.
results.boring: The 'no action' rate (65% on tribal land) is mostly paperwork habit. Most of those violations carry a 'compliance achieved' close-out (SOX/EOX), and states log a notice letter where EPA regions don't. So I led with the unaddressed-today rate instead. Slow data entry could still inflate that rate; not ruled out. Portland and Jackson MS are known stories. The MT0002988 severity pile was not checked (budget).
traps: A violation repeats once per enforcement action: dedupe on PWSID+VIOLATION_ID or counts triple
'No enforcement' mostly means only a Resolving close-out (SOX/EOX); every Resolved violation carries one
Code 5200 unaddressed rows start 2024-10-17 (the lead-pipe inventory deadline) and inflate health-based unaddressed counts; split it out
1.0M rows are enforcement-only with no VIOLATION_ID; about 25.5K rows carry 99999... placeholder ENFORCEMENT_IDs
Contaminant codes (0700, 0800, 5000, 5200) need the EPA lookup; my readings of them are inferences

results.headline: 2,776 of 16,443 high-hazard dams are rated Poor or Unsatisfactory (16.9%). 753 of those have the emergency-plan flag set to False (27%), against about 95% plan coverage on Satisfactory ones. Kentucky: 91 of 106. New Mexico: 94 of 145. BIA owns 60 of the bad dams.
results.checked: I filtered to HAZARD_POTENTIAL='High' and CONDITION_ASSESSMENT Poor or Unsatisfactory, and dropped associated structures. I grouped by owner type and by state, listed the top owners and the largest Unsatisfactory dams, and listed the BIA dams. To test the inspection angle, I compared good and bad dams' years since inspection within each state. I also counted the values of the plan flag.
results.hit_means: 753 dams could fail and kill people with no written warning plan, clustered in KY, NM, NC and SC. The list is named and checkable against the state dam-safety offices.
results.miss_means: If the False flags turn out to mean 'not reported', the count shrinks to a list of states that don't report.
results.boring: AP counted poor high-hazard dams in 2019 (1,688; different method, so no trend claim). The years-since-inspection angle is killed: in GA, IN and PA, good and bad dams show the same median years (9.6 vs 9.7, 7.2 vs 7.9, 5.9 vs 5.9), and those states' records are about 1,950 days old, so it is reporting lag. The plan flag has no NULLs, so 'not reported' may be folded into False; not ruled out. Federal dams are 78.4% unrated, so federal counts are floors.
traps: LAST_INSPECTION_DATE is only as fresh as the state's last NID upload; GA, IN and PA records have a median age of about 5.3 years
HAS_EMERGENCY_ACTION_PLAN is TRUE/FALSE only with no NULL, so False may mean not reported; 33 'no plan' rows carry a plan revision date
Federal high-hazard dams are 78.4% Not Rated, Not Available or blank, so counts are floors
Drop IS_ASSOCIATED_STRUCTURE rows or dams double
Junk dates: inspection dates as late as 5023-05-25, 1901-01-01 placeholders, 1980-01-01 on 1,599 rows; STATE is spelled out (Texas), not two letters

results.headline: 19 active community water systems serving 10K+ people are over the lead action level on their latest test (2024-25), serving 724,514 people. 7 of the 19 are in Illinois, including Elgin (53 ppb, over in 7 of 13 periods) and Aurora (183K people, 24 ppb). Triage's 370K 'lead' max is copper junk.
results.checked: I took the 90th-percentile lead rows (PB90) and kept one value per system per period for periods ending 2015-01-01 to today. I counted readings over 0.015 mg/L, capped at 1 mg/L to drop ppb typed as mg/L, and joined the water-systems table for name, type and population. Then I compared peers by type and size band and pulled the latest reading for active community systems of 10K+. Before any of that, I checked units by value band and by state.
results.hit_means: A named town is over the action level on its latest test, with a cluster in one state's suburbs. That is a current story, not a Flint rerun.
results.miss_means: Without the Illinois cluster this is a history list: 497 systems over in 3+ periods (4.25M people), topped by Newark, Pittsburgh, Providence, Boston-area MWRA towns, Portland and Jackson, which are already covered and mostly under 15 ppb now.
results.boring: The persistent list is the known cities; not ruled out, that is the explanation for that list. The Illinois cluster may be a change in how systems sample, not worse water; unchecked. For a tiny system, the 90th percentile of 5 samples is basically the worst tap. Big systems test every 6 months and small ones every 3 years, so period counts don't compare across sizes. Peers: small non-community systems (schools, plants) have the highest share ever over, 12.5-12.7%, against 3.6-8.6% for community systems.
traps: SAMPLE_MEASURE mixes lead (PB90) and copper (CU90); the 370,000 max is copper at KS2013505, and 144 copper rows over 1,000 are whole-number junk
2,314 lead rows between 1 and 15 'mg/L' are ppb in a mg/L column, mostly Ohio and before 2015; since 2015 no state has more than 0.7% of rows above 1
Never sum SAMPLE_MEASURE across CONTAMINANT_CODE; the triage's '94% in the top 1%' comes from the copper junk
About 2,090 lead rows have period end dates after today (scheduled periods)

results.headline: 16.2% of chemical rows nationally are hidden as trade secrets. Diamondback hides 30.3% in Texas (state rate 16.2%) and has secrets in 96.7% of its 3,164 jobs. QEP (WY), Chesapeake (TX, OK, OH) and Cimarex run 10-14 points above their own states. There are no job dates at all, so no drought angle.
results.checked: I rolled up to one row per disclosure first. Secret share = rows marked PROPRIETARY, CONFIDENTIAL, TRADE SECRET, CONFIDENTIAL BUSINES or CBI, divided by rows with a non-blank CAS field. I compared each operator-state to its own state's share. Water per job was deduped per disclosure. I also checked depth outliers and repeat filings.
results.hit_means: A driller hiding twice its state's rate across nearly every job is a named outlier worth asking about.
results.miss_means: If everyone sat near 16%, secrecy would just be the industry norm with no outlier to name.
results.boring: Trade-secret claims are legal and industry-wide, and advocacy reports have covered them. The facts line's TVD and water sums are dead: both repeat on every ingredient row (0 of 248,835 disclosures vary), the Clayton Williams max depth is 1.19B ft, and 74 jobs claim more than 40K ft. The drought angle can't be done because there are no dates.
traps: JOB_START_DATE and JOB_END_DATE are empty on all 7.2M rows
TOTAL_BASE_WATER_VOLUME and TVD repeat on every ingredient row; dedupe to one row per DISCLOSURE_ID
TVD over 40,000 ft on 74 disclosures; the max is 1.19B ft
Secret markers are spelled at least 5 ways, and 899K CAS fields are blank
Operator names are not merged (Chesapeake, Anadarko appear per state); 12,203 disclosures are repeat filings on an already-disclosed well

results.headline: The top 1% of TRI sites (218) put out 81.6% of 2023's 2.98B lb on-site release. Metal mines put out 50.4%, and one mine, Red Dog (Teck, AK), put out 25.9% (771M lb). This is EPA's own annual headline.
results.checked: I used pounds rows only: Form A rows are zero by design and 770 dioxin rows are in grams. I summed C_65_ON_SITE_RELEASE_TOTAL per facility, then per sector, and took the top-1% share. I also ranked the non-mining carcinogen air releases (stack plus fugitive).
results.hit_means: A non-mining plant at the very top would be a named-plant story.
results.miss_means: Mines on top means this is the known annual story, and that is what came back.
results.boring: Mines count moved waste rock as a release; confirmed as the reason for the ranking. Non-mining leads: hydrogen sulfide at gas plants (Dark Horse Treating, Jal NM, 73.6M lb; Targa Midway 42.0M lb) may be acid gas pumped underground and counted as a release; unchecked. Carcinogen air is topped by styrene from fiberglass boat and bathtub makers (Onyx Collection KS, 751,599 lb). Whether the sites are near people was not tested (needs a census join).
traps: Form A rows (8,838) carry 0 release by design, not clean sites
770 dioxin rows are in Grams; don't add them to pounds
The C_46 carcinogen flag includes styrene, so boat and bathtub makers top 'carcinogen air'
Section 5 release columns are text; C_65 and C_107 are floats
C_14_HORIZONTAL_DATUM is empty

results.headline: Split by state, the minority gap flips: long violators in minority areas are worse off in 8 states, better off in 10, tied in 1. The 'never fined / never inspected' flags are mostly drinking-water systems and time-window effects.
results.checked: Counted every flag and tested it against the columns it summarizes. Pulled each facility's drinking-water flag from ECHO by FRS_ID (all 93,808 matched). For facilities with 8+ bad quarters out of 12, split by program and neighborhood minority band: share never fined (LAST_PENALTY_AMT_ALLOCATED = 0) over the long violators in that band, and share with no inspection date on record, same denominator. Then compared each state with itself: 50%+ minority areas against under-25% areas.
results.hit_means: Within the same state and program, long violators in minority areas go unfined or uninspected more often. That would be a real environmental-justice story.
results.miss_means: The national gap is which states the facilities sit in. Fines show no gradient: air runs backwards (35.7% never fined in under-10% minority areas, 25.6% in 75%+ areas); water is 82.5% to 83.6%. The no-inspection gap (water 16.7% to 35.7%) splits 8 states up, 10 down, 1 tied.
results.boring: Confirmed. State programs record differently: Georgia (67%/63%) and Colorado (62%/55%) lack inspection dates whatever the neighborhood. Drinking-water systems are 38,522 rows (41%), 21,634 of the 53,437 long violators and 19,994 of the 'no fine, no inspection' rows. The 12-of-12, never-fined list is mostly small-town sewage plants and mobile-home parks. A few industrial names (SK Battery America GA, Stella-Jones PA, ARI Railcar GA) are data matches, not verified.
traps: CHRONIC_NO_PENALTY is true on 5,322 facilities that have a past penalty in LAST_PENALTY_AMT (e.g. North & Judd CT, $100K in 1994)
NEVER_INSPECTED_NONCOMPLIANT is true on 12,282 facilities that have a DATE_LAST_INSPECTION; TOTAL_INSPECTION_COUNT covers only about the last 5 years
38,522 rows (41%) have no air, water or hazwaste flag; all are drinking-water systems in ECHO
PCT_MINORITY is blank on 29,702 rows (32%), mostly the drinking-water rows
LAST_PENALTY_SHARED_FACILITY_N = 3013568 on 78,315 rows, never on a row with a penalty: a filler value

results.headline: Penalties vary 20-40x between states, but the biggest driver is what each state reports into this federal file. The clean peer number is Oklahoma refineries at $3.3K penalty per logged violation against Texas at $142K, on only 9 facilities.
results.checked: Grouped by ENF_IDENTIFIER to find penalties copied across facilities. Listed the top cases with each penalty counted once. By state, 2015-2025, one row per case per state: share of cases with a penalty and median penalty per penalized case, for all sources and for major sources. Listed repeat facilities. Built a refinery peer group (NAICS 324110): penalty per refinery-coded facility, and penalty per violation logged in the violation-history table.
results.hit_means: The same kind of plant, breaking rules at the same logged rate, pays far less in one state than another.
results.miss_means: The gaps reflect what each state logs, not what it charges. California local districts log 2,216 refinery violations and 1,551 cases; Louisiana logs 6 violations against 85 cases for 38 refinery-coded sites.
results.boring: Not ruled out. California districts log every notice of violation (Kern Oil: 532 cases, median $8,625). EPA-heavy states show bigger medians (OH 36.6% EPA, median $50,850 for major sources; TN $3,000). National settlements sit on one facility row: the $100.7M max is EES Coke Battery MI and $64.5M is Henry Charging ND well pads. Refinery-coded facilities include small units and nothing is weighted by plant size.
traps: 395 multi-facility cases copy the same penalty onto every facility (1,767 rows): raw sum $5.81B, each case once $3.86B, so $1.95B (34%) is repeats
NM000A200275488 (Magnum Compressor Station NM) puts $31.6M on 11 facilities = $347.7M raw
ICIS-Air state coverage is uneven: Ohio logged 347 formal cases 2015-2025 against Indiana's 1,176

results.headline: The 'states let high-priority violators ride' angle measures which states report into ICIS-Air: 558 of 8,896 HPVs from 2012-2021 (6.3%) never drew a formal action, and the state outliers are reporting gaps.
results.checked: Took high-priority violations (HPVs) that started 2012-2021, giving each 4+ years to be acted on, one row per determination. Joined formal actions for the same PGM_SYS_ID, aggregated per case first. By state: share still unresolved, median days to resolve, share with a formal action within 2 years, share with none ever after the start date. Listed the oldest open HPVs with no action, with the facility file's operating status.
results.hit_means: Specific states sit on serious air violations for years and never act.
results.miss_means: The gaps sit where formal actions or violations never reach this federal file. Ohio (53.4% of 133 HPVs with no formal action) and Wisconsin (56.6% of 113) report few formal cases; Louisiana reports almost no violations.
results.boring: Confirmed. Ohio logged 347 formal cases to Indiana's 1,176; Louisiana refineries logged 6 violations against 85 formal cases. California holds 52% of HPVs (4,659) because its local districts log everything. The 173 open HPVs with no action include plants the file lists as permanently closed and known names (Greka Energy Cat Canyon). Michigan's 64.4% unresolved (101 HPVs, median 1,830 days to resolve) is parked, not explained.
traps: COMP_DETERMINATION_UID is unique on every row (57,250 of 57,250 FRV, 44,787 of 44,787 HPV); the facts.tsv '751 repeats' and the triage warning built on it are wrong
134 HPV start dates fall before 1990 (earliest in year 0218), 474 HPVs are 'resolved' before they started, and one start date (2026-09-28) is after today
A missing formal action or violation here usually means a state did not report, not that nothing happened

results.headline: The famous $6.7B is two identical $3.35B lines under two EPA region case numbers. With BP set aside, the biggest water fines are a Texas recycler ($57M), a bankruptcy claim ($39M) and a likely typo ($30M).
results.checked: Grouped by ENF_IDENTIFIER to find penalties repeated across permits. Listed top cases with each counted once. Read every row on GMG290110 and on TN0021547. By state, 2015-2026, BP case removed: share of cases with a penalty and median penalty per penalized case, over 32,983 case-state rows. Listed the permits with the most formal cases, penalty counted once per case.
results.hit_means: A state or permit holder that racks up formal actions while fines stay at zero, compared with peers.
results.miss_means: What counts as a formal action differs by state, so per-case comparisons compare paperwork styles. North Carolina logs every monthly limit-breach penalty (4,520 cases, 99.2% penalized, median $787), so the top 20 repeat permits are all small North Carolina plants. Pace Mobile Home Park had 80 cases worth $226K.
results.boring: Partly confirmed. BP is famous, and its two lines are 04-2010-9036 and 06-2011-4881, both on 2012-06-18, both $3,352,250,000. That looks like one settlement logged twice or split in halves; not checked against the consent decree. The 10-12% penalized shares (OK 12.2%, IL 10.0%) may mean orders are logged here and penalties land elsewhere; not ruled out. Lead: Altair Recycling Facility TX, $57.0M state civil judicial on 2025-06-06, also has open RCRA violations. Data match, not verified.
traps: Case penalties repeat across permits: federal amount identical in 258 multi-permit cases, state amount in 998; federal raw $8.13B vs $6.99B each case once, state raw $1.50B vs $0.86B (43% repeats)
Martin County Coal case 04-2006-9037 puts $6.7M on 76 permits = $509.2M raw
Jonesborough STP TN (TN0021547) shows a $30,000,000 state penalty in 2009; its only other penalty was $600, so likely a typo
The federal penalty column is filled on only 4.0% of rows (4,533); the state column on 42.8%

results.headline: Almost every hazardous-waste violation gets a fix date. Only 2,247 violations at 715 handlers from 1980-2020 are still open, out of 614K+, and 222 of those handlers still carry an EPA flag in 2026.
results.checked: Measured the share with no ACTUAL_RTC_DATE by the 5-year bucket each violation was found in. Counted open violations found 1980-2020 by handler. Joined names from RCRA_FACILITIES, then EPA's own monthly flag file (RCRA_VIOSNC_HISTORY) as a second check on whether each site is still in trouble. By state, 2010-2020: share open, share with a due date, share fixed after the due date, median days late.
results.hit_means: Live hazardous-waste handlers sitting on found violations for years, still flagged by EPA today.
results.miss_means: Open violations are rare: 0.0-0.4% open for every bucket from 1980 to 2014. The old ones are closed, bankrupt or cleanup sites where nobody records a fix.
results.boring: Partly confirmed. The open pool is tiny, and the oldest names read like abandoned or cleanup sites (Dynachem IL, Chemetco IL, US Oil Recovery TX). The 5.4% open for 2020-24 and 19.7% for 2025-26 is ordinary lag. Most violations are generator paperwork (262.A 189K rows, 262.C 113K). Still flagged in 2026: City Foundry San Antonio (open since 1995), Clean Harbors of Colfax LA, Altair Recycling TX, Santolubes SC. Data matches, not verified.
traps: SCHEDULED_COMPLIANCE_DATE is state practice: filled mostly in WA, WI, KY and GA and near 0% in TX, OH, FL and PA, so days overdue only works in a few states
RCRA_VIOSNC_HISTORY holds only flagged months with three pairs (Y/N, Y/Y, N/Y); 'N/Y' (serious noncomplier but not in violation) is unexplained, so the columns may be swapped
184 of the 715 open-violation handlers never appear in the flag file at all

results.headline: 19 police, fire, veteran and cancer 527s spent $201.8M from 2014 to 2026: 74% went to fundraising-type purposes, $0.2M to candidates. Four of them share a Delafield or Brookfield, WI address ($114.7M), and nine share one template (exactly 90% fundraising, BFTELECOM LLC as top payee). The triage question, who gets the $13.3B, lands on card processors and party ad buyers, which is boring.
results.checked: 8,191,177 rows, $13.316B, 3,313 EINs. I dropped cross-form copies (the same EIN + payee + date + amount on 2+ forms): $2.02B, leaving $11.269B. Then I summed payees, matched payee names to officers of the same group, split each group's spending into fundraising-type vs contribution purposes (keyword match, checked against the raw purpose text on 9 groups), and pulled custodians and addresses from the 8872 reports for the 19 groups that are over 50% fundraising.
results.hit_means: A network of charity-sounding 527s, tied by shared addresses (2301 Sun Valley Dr, Delafield WI), shared custodians (Nile Porter; Pulciani/Nizick; Greenlee) and shared telemarketers (Residential Programs Inc, BFTELECOM), sending most of $200M to fundraisers. It sits on IRS forms, outside the FEC data most scam-PAC trackers use. All names are data matches, not verified against primary records.
results.miss_means: If the groups are already named in the FEC scam-PAC coverage, it's a known story with new IRS-side numbers. Payee = officer is only $79.7M (0.7%), all salary and reimbursements. Payees paid by both parties are American Express and Paychex. The top payees are processors (Stripe $173.8M) and partisan ad buyers (Target Enterprises $152.3M, Great American Media $141.8M).
results.boring: Scam PACs are a known genre: CNN 2020, the Daily Beast's $140M network story, Jacobin 2024 and The Lever, mostly from FEC data. Telemarketing-heavy spending is legal. Not ruled out that some of these groups are already covered. The triage 'boring' is confirmed for the top payees: governors-association ad buyers and payment processors.
traps: $2.02B of cross-form amendment copies; dedup on EIN + payee + date + amount, keeping the biggest single-form count
The $1.47B lump-row trap is Schedule A; lump-named rows on Schedule B total about $0.3B (ActBlue 'SUM OF TRANSACTIONS', RGA 'TOTAL SCHEDULE B EXPENDITURES')
ActBlue Non-Federal is 6.7M rows (82%), a $25-median pass-through to state candidates; it sets the table median
ORG_NAME drifts within one EIN (822366231 shows as both Firefighters Support Fund and Firefighters and EMS Fund)

results.headline: 2024 Senate general independent spending: $675.2M backed the winning side, $516.1M backed the loser (43% of the $1,191.3M scored). WinSenate put 59% ($177.9M) on the losing side; SLF PAC put 29% there. The House can't be scored because WHO_WON stops at 2018.
results.checked: 866,730 rows, cycles 2024 and 2026, 18,643 memo rows dropped. Split 24E (for) and 24A (against) by committee, with names from COMMITTEES_DIM. Joined candidate IDs to the 2024 FEC candidate file, then to WHO_WON 2024 on state + office + district + surname. Second field: party matched on 30 of 32 winners and 24 of 25 runners-up.
results.hit_means: A per-committee 'money on the losing side' scorecard. For example: Last Best Place PAC 100% ($29.1M), Maryland's Future 100% ($27.0M), NRSC 99% ($21.2M). Biggest against-money on candidates who won anyway: McCormick $79.2M, Moreno $76.4M.
results.miss_means: House races (most of the candidates) can't be scored until WHO_WON gets 2020-2024 House results. Presidential results end in 2016 too.
results.boring: The money is the famous super PACs: FF PAC $502.6M, MAGA Inc $319.3M against, WinSenate, CLF, SLF, HMP. Money flows to toss-ups, so a near 50/50 split is expected, and press scorecards exist. Holds.
traps: POLITICS__WHO_WON: House ends 2018, President ends 2016, Senate reaches 2024
24K direct contributions ($508.6M in 2024) sit in the same table as IE; filter TRANSACTION_TP
FEC candidate file has multiple rows per CAND_ID; filter CAND_ELECTION_YR

results.headline: County density per person is big: Forest PA has 1,685 wells per 10K people, Monroe OH 1,491, Nowata OK 1,441. Venango PA holds 4,786 wells (25% of PA's). The operator angle is dead: no operator column exists.
results.checked: 117,672 rows, 117,669 distinct WELL_IDENTIFIER (only 3 IDs repeat, twice each). 27 states, one file each, dated 2019-07 to 2022-12. Counted distinct wells by state and county, took each county's share of its own state, and joined to DIM_COUNTY 2020 population (99.1% of wells landed). Searched the notes for operator names and read the STATUS values per state.
results.hit_means: A per-person orphan-well map for rural Appalachia and Oklahoma, compared within each state.
results.miss_means: No operator names: only 'Operator Unknown' on 3,594 West Virginia rows. The snapshot predates most federal plugging money, and state lists mix idle, plugged and not-found wells, so there's no 'who left them' story.
results.boring: Counts reflect how hard each state documented its wells. Appalachian orphan wells are widely reported. Not ruled out. The triage's load-duplicate explanation is ruled out: the 434-row repeats don't exist.
traps: The '434-row repeated API ids' in facts.tsv is an APPROX_TOP_K artifact; the real max is 2
STATUS is not 'orphan': CA 3,173 of 3,338 Idle (plus 126 Plugged, 36 Active); NY 2,085 'Unknown Not Found'; OH 15,493 of 20,557 'HP'; CO 186 of 409 'PA'; TX blank on all 5,854
One snapshot per state, 2019-2022; stale

results.headline: Peer outliers exist. CSX plus Norfolk Southern made 8.2x the NRC calls per year of UP plus BNSF in 2015-17, down to 1.8x by 2024-25. Cox Operating logged 404 calls in 2021-23 against Chevron's 283 nationwide. But the table is call headers only, with no material, amount or spill location.
results.checked: 1,029,020 rows, one per SEQNOS, 1990 to 2026-08. Counted calls by year, the blank-company share and the SEQNOS range. Grouped company names into families by prefix (railroads, Gulf offshore, majors, pipelines) for 2015-2025 and compared each family within its peer group.
results.hit_means: Named companies to chase: the eastern railroads' call rate, and Cox Operating's 2018-23 surge (726 calls, then 20 in 2024-25).
results.miss_means: A call can't be sized without the material and amount sheets, and those aren't in the warehouse. 47.5% of calls since 2015 (132,073 of 277,988) name no company.
results.boring: These are self-reported calls, and reporting habits differ by company. CSX's 75% drop in yearly calls could be a change in who phones it in. Taylor Energy's MC-20 leak is well known. Not ruled out. The triage's 'SEQNOS 999999 sentinel' is false: SEQNOS is unique and runs 1 to 1,469,629.
traps: facts.tsv 'SEQNOS 999999 4.0K' is an APPROX_TOP_K artifact; '999999' appears on 1 row
No material, quantity or incident-location columns loaded; RESPONSIBLE_CITY is the company's address, not the spill site
The blank-company share rose from 19.4% (1990) to 49.8% (2025)
Chevron's 6.7K + 4.1K in triage covers all years; since 2015 the Chevron family is 1,174 calls across 79 spellings

results.headline: Data set 10's pager fell from 10,071 pages (~503.6K files) to 5,569 (~278.5K) on 2026-03-11 and held for 10 snapshots through May. But DS9 and DS11 made drops just as big that later reverted, so no drop can be called a removal from this table.
results.checked: Pulled all 339 snapshots (12 pages, 2025-12-19 to 2026-06-03) and ordered each page by time. Checked that APPROX_FILES = PAGER_PAGES x 50 on every row. Listed every change in pager pages and in files on page one.
results.hit_means: If a direct re-crawl of DS10's file links confirms about 225K fewer files, that's a disappearance on the record.
results.miss_means: It's the same glitch as DS11, whose month-long 5,549 reading went back to 6,634, and DS9 (10,678 → 770 → 10,675).
results.boring: Pager parse glitches, confirmed: a '2 pages' reading appears at random on 10 of 12 pages. A site template change explains page-one counts falling by exactly one on 9 of 12 pages the week of 2026-02-03; on a multi-page list, a removed file can't shrink page one. The only file-level blip: DS6 lost one file from 2026-02-10 to 2026-03-19.
traps: APPROX_FILES_FROM_PAGER is just PAGER_PAGES x 50; '2' is a glitch value
The 533.9K max is DS9 at 10,678 pages, one of the swinging readings
FILES_ON_PAGE_ONE shifted by one site-wide the week of 2026-02-03 (template change)
57 of 339 pager fields blank; DS6 and DS7 have no pager

results.headline: 54 home health owners with 5%+ stakes share a first name, last name and state with someone on the OIG exclusion list, where chance predicts 20.8. After dropping middle-initial conflicts, 44 people are left. 54 of their 55 agencies are still on Care Compare, and 12 are LA-area agencies certified 2023-25 (12 of 941 new CA agencies, 1.3%, against 0.44% of all agencies nationally). All names are data matches, not verified against primary records.
results.checked: Counted distinct agencies per owner ID (ownership roles 34/35 only), top 25 people and top 25 companies. For each state, took the share of agencies with a 3+-agency individual owner. Joined owners to the OIG exclusion list on first name + last name + state, also company name + state and agency NPI. Chance baseline: owners whose name is anywhere on the list, same-state hits against that state's share of the list (11,611 owner-states, 349 names on the list, 54 in the same state, 20.8 expected). Dropped middle-initial conflicts, which left 44 people at 55 agencies, 33 of them with the exclusion dated before the latest ownership date. Looked the 55 agencies up on Care Compare for listing, stars and spend per episode against their state.
results.hit_means: CMS's own current owner file lists people the OIG barred from federal health programs, and their agencies are still enrolled, running through the LA new-agency boom (CA holds 941 of the 1,606 agencies certified since 2023). Examples: Artur Harutyunyan (excluded 2014, owner of 2 agencies 2020/2023); Kristine Arutyunyan (excluded 2024-01, still listed through 2026-04); Arman Danielian (excluded 2026-01, still owner of 3 agencies). In FL, 3 matched agencies sit in the state's top 1% for Medicare spend per episode (1.31-1.35x national).
results.miss_means: The matches are name collisions. The exclusion list has no birth date and these people have no NPI, so name plus state is the whole join. Each row needs its court record (case number, defendant age, named business) before it counts.
results.boring: NOT ruled out: names cluster by place (Armenian surnames in LA, Hispanic names in FL/TX), which raises chance same-state hits above the 20.8 baseline, so the true excess is under 33. City can't serve as a second check: only 9 of 141 rows agree on city, and the exclusion-list address is often a prison town (Coleman FL, Beaumont TX). Big chains owning hundreds (UnitedHealth 355, LHC 297) are legit and aren't the story. RULED OUT: the triage worry about 85.6K null CCNs. CCN is 98% filled (99,287 of 101,188). No LA/Houston owner-network cluster shows by owner ID (CA 4.9% and TX 4.0% of agencies have a 3+-agency individual owner, against 3.4% nationally, 6.4% in CO and 6.3% in OK). The hospice half of the angle can't be tested because no hospice owner file is landed.
traps: The triage 'boring' line misread the facts: CCN is 98% filled (99,287/101,188); 85.6K was a sum of ownership percents
The exclusion list's CITY is the address at exclusion, often a prison town, so it can't be a second-field check on a name match
No hospice owner file is landed (LANDING has FED_CMS_HOSPICE and FED_CMS_HOSPICE_ENROLLMENTS only), so 'same owners run hospices' needs a load

results.headline: Against their own states, chains run at a median of 1.00x fire citations per home and a max of 1.95x; 22 of 301 chains sit at 1.5x or more. CareCore Health (OH, 12 homes, 1.95x, 11 of 12 homes repeat a tag all 3 cycles, 2.54x state rate), Aperion Care (IL/IN, 33 homes, 1.76x, 22 of 33 repeat, 1.83x) and Eden Senior Care (16 of 19 repeat, 2.2x) lead. It's almost all sprinkler and alarm testing (K0353, K0345), with 0-1 G+ citations per chain.
results.checked: Joined CCN to the nursing home file's CHAIN_NAME (every fire CCN matched). For each chain with 10+ homes, counted fire/emergency citations over the 3 cycles, with zero-citation homes in the denominator, against an expected count built from each home's state average. Did the same for F+ severity and the core tags (K0351/0353/0372/0374/0918), and for homes cited for the same tag in all 3 cycles (national share 27.4%). Pulled the states and top tags for the leaders.
results.hit_means: A few mostly one-state chains let sprinkler and alarm testing lapse at home after home, cycle after cycle, at up to 2.5x their state peers. Bria (IL, 1.79x) ties to F-029.
results.miss_means: The spread is narrow (90th percentile 1.43x), and chains of 12-19 homes can hit 2x by chance. Severity is low: 215 of 200,030 rows are G or worse.
results.boring: State inspection intensity is ruled out by comparing each chain with its own states. Building age is NOT ruled out: old buildings draw more K-tags. The top tags are upkeep and paperwork. The big chains sit near 1.0x (Ensign 0.80, PACS 1.15, Life Care 1.04, Genesis 1.03). Arcadia (F-021's worst chain for fines) is 1.06x, so there's no tie to F-021.
traps: 200,030 rows is not a cap: every row is a unique home, date and tag, over 3 inspection cycles

results.headline: In 2024, against their own states, DaVita's deaths ran 1.021x CMS expected (about 650 extra of 31,545), Fresenius 0.965x (about 1,160 fewer of 32,050), and independents were worst at 1.102x. Hospital admissions: 1.020, 0.971 and 1.047. Share of clinics significantly worse on deaths: 2.9%, 2.3% and 5.3%.
results.checked: Pivoted the 2024 measures for each clinic: deaths (deay4_f), expected deaths (exdy4_f), SMR, p-value, admissions (htay4_f), expected admissions (exty4_f), SHR and p-value. Pooled observed over expected by chain (20+ clinics), then re-based on each clinic's state pooled ratio. Flagged worse as ratio above 1 with p under 0.05. Joined the infection ratio from HEALTH__FED_CMS_DIALYSIS (median SIR: DaVita 0.25, Fresenius 0.26, independents 0.43).
results.hit_means: DaVita runs about 6% above Fresenius on deaths and 5% on admissions, for patients CMS has already risk-adjusted.
results.miss_means: The chains sit within a few percent of each other, and the significant flags are rare everywhere (2-5%).
results.boring: The expected counts already adjust for patient mix, so a gap of about 6% is real but small. Chain quality was covered by ProPublica in 2010. Independents are a mix of hospital-based and rural clinics. Mostly confirmed: too small and too known to lead.
traps: There are 2,678 MEASURE_IDs and the ID carries the year (smry4_f = 2024 SMR); MEASURE_SCORE mixes counts, percents, ratios, p-values and ranks
This table has no 2024 bloodstream infection ratio (only a PD catheter infection rate, for 1,272 clinics); use STANDARD_INFECTION_RATIO in HEALTH__FED_CMS_DIALYSIS

results.headline: In 2024, of 308,054 consecutive price steps on same-unit generics, 127 were 2x+ up, only 20 were 3x+ up (7 drug groups, 3 of them OTC), and 542 halved. The real jumps: acetaminophen-codeine solution 30x ($0.0145 to $0.434/mL), hydrocodone-APAP solution 5.6x, naproxen DR 375 mg 4.9x, and saxagliptin 5 mg 4.2x then 4.9x ($1.35 to $6.67/tab). The 2022-23 window isn't in the warehouse.
results.checked: For each NDC, compared each price with the one before it (LAG over effective date). Kept generics (G) with an unchanged pricing unit. Counted 2x/3x step-ups and halvings. Grouped the jumps by drug, counting the NDCs that moved and whether the next price fell back. Counted rows with effective dates before 2024.
results.hit_means: A handful of old generics repriced several-fold overnight, and saxagliptin and the opioid solutions held their new prices.
results.miss_means: Several-fold jumps are rare (20 in a year) and small in dollars. Many 2x steps revert within a month (phenobarbital, dexmethylphenidate).
results.boring: Makers exiting and shortages (methylphenidate shows at 2x) explain most of it, and generic spikes were big news in 2014-16. The per-unit and package-size fakes are ruled out by requiring the same unit. The 2022-23 part of the angle is unresolved, not empty: those files aren't loaded.
traps: NADAC holds only the 52 weekly files of 2024. Effective dates before 2024 are one carried-in starting price per NDC (26,600 rows, 26,587 NDCs), not a 2022-23 series
A NADAC generic price is set for the whole drug group: all NDCs in a group move by the same ratio, so NDC count is not independent confirmation

results.headline: High-charge hospitals bill up to 4.39x their state's median for the same DRG (Capital Health Regional NJ: 41 of 46 DRGs at 3x+), but Medicare pays them 0.83-1.24x the median. The hospitals Medicare pays 2-5x the median are public safety-net hospitals: Parkland 5.07x ($44.9M above median), JPS 3.87x, Kings County 2.82x, Jackson Memorial 2.03x ($50.6M).
results.checked: For each state and DRG with 5+ hospitals, took the median billed charge and median Medicare payment. For each hospital with 20+ DRGs, took its median charge ratio and median payment ratio against those medians, plus discharge-weighted dollars above the median. Totals: 145,879 rows, 2,906 hospitals, 540 DRGs, 4,952,481 discharges, $75.1B Medicare paid against $457.6B billed (6.1x).
results.hit_means: Medicare pays some hospitals far more per case for the same DRG.
results.miss_means: Charges are list prices that don't move Medicare payment, and the data shows it: the high-charge hospitals get paid about the median.
results.boring: This fits the data. The high-payment list is exactly the public safety-net list, which is what the teaching, disproportionate-share and outlier add-ons in the payment column predict. That isn't separable with this table, and CMS's method note wasn't re-checked. The charge gaps are the 2013 chargemaster story.
traps: The table has no year column, so the data year can't be read from the table

results.headline: Lower Brule Sioux Tribe (data match, not verified): going-concern doubt 10 of 10 audit years (2016-2025) and material noncompliance 10 of 10, while federal spending went from $16.7M to $35.7M ($246.2M over 10 years).
results.checked: 411,638 reports, one per report ID; 68,128 EINs; audit years 2016-2026. Flags hold Yes, No or GSA_MIGRATION. Grouped by EIN and audit year, states left out, then counted the years carrying each flag. Going concern 3+ years: 362 of 48,202 auditees with 3+ audited years (0.75%). Tribes: 13 of 827. Material weakness 5+ straight years: tribes 83 of 822 (10.1%), local 268 of 14,441 (1.9%), non-profit 180 of 22,009 (0.8%). Read Lower Brule row by row: one EIN, the same auditor (REDW) since 2017, qualified or adverse opinions 2019-22. Hope the Mission (LA): going concern and material weakness all 3 years 2022-24, $150.6M.
results.hit_means: A named group got federal money every year while its own auditor doubted it could survive and flagged it for breaking the rules, and the money grew. Only 3 tribes reach 10+ going-concern-plus-noncompliance flag-years: Lower Brule at 20, and two Pine Ridge schools (Loneman 12, Porcupine 10).
results.miss_means: The flags would be boilerplate or artifacts. The row check rules that out for Lower Brule.
results.boring: Tribal, Medicaid and school money is mostly formula money, so agencies often can't cut it over audit flags. Not ruled out, and that's the story's hinge. The top dollars in going-concern years belong to known cases: Brazos ($24.9B, a student-loan program winding down, where loan balances count as spending), Puerto Rico agencies, and NYC safety-net hospitals (Jamaica 9/9, Wyckoff 9/9). The 80% top-1% share is states, and states are dropped here.
traps: Material weakness rate goes from 5.2-6.2% on Census reports (2016-22) to 14.5% and 14.0% on GSA FAC (2023-24). A streak across 2022-2023 is not like-for-like.
47 rows are typed 'local' but named 'State of ...' (State of Arizona at $24.7B a year). Dropping 'state' doesn't drop all states.
EIN 660433481 carries 8 auditee names. One EIN is not always one group.
No findings or questioned-costs table in the warehouse, so 'repeat finding' and 'questioned costs' can't be tested.

results.headline: Complaints joined to recalls reproduce known scandals: Jeep fuel system had 8 fatal complaints (25 deaths) filed 13.1 years before the 2014 recall; GM Cobalt 13 fatal complaints 8.8 years early; Takata/Honda 21 fatal 14.7 years early. Nothing new at the top.
results.checked: 2,227,941 rows = 1,607,298 complaints (ODINO repeats once per component). Deaths counted once per complaint with 99s dropped: 4,388 on about 2,850 fatal complaints. The 8.6K in facts is about 2x from row repeats. Joined harm complaints to vehicle recalls on make + model + model year + component head (text before : and ,), keeping complaints received before the owner-notice date, once per campaign. Then split fatal complaints by whether their model year ever got a recall on that component, and read the complaint text behind three leads.
results.hit_means: Complaints about dead people sat on file for years before the maker recalled that part. The top list (Takata, GM ignition switch, Jeep fuel tanks, Toyota sudden acceleration, Tesla driver-assist) shows the join works.
results.miss_means: Nothing new sits above the known scandals, and that's what happened. The leads that were new collapsed when I read the text.
results.boring: A component match is loose: an air-bag death complaint can be a bag that didn't deploy. Lincoln MKS '54 deaths' is one family filing the same 2 deaths 7 times, plus a junk row with DEATHS=40. Tesla Model S suspension's 11 fatal complaints read like one filer posting news links and junkyard listings. Only 41.2% of fatal complaints match any vehicle recall at all. Ford Explorer tires (82 fatal) is Firestone, recalled as equipment, so 'never recalled' is absence, not a finding. Ruled out as a new story.
traps: DEATHS summed over rows double counts, because ODINO repeats per component. Take MAX per ODINO.
Junk death values under 99 exist (40 deaths and 38 injured on one link-only row). Dropping 99 is not enough.
Repeat filers: one family or one person can file the same death many times.
The 'no recall' side is unreliable: a vehicle-only filter misses tire and equipment recalls, and only 41% of fatal complaints match any recall on make, model and year.

results.headline: Mercedes' 28.66B units is really 9.40M. Campaign 21V058000 repeats 1,292,258 units on 18,662 rows (24.1B by itself). The real top is Ford at 94.3M units in 760 campaigns. On re-recalls, Tesla is 24% vs about 3-15% for peers.
results.checked: 241,861 rows, 15,116 campaigns. Affected units never vary inside a campaign (0 exceptions), and no campaign spans two makers. Summed units once per campaign, by maker key (first word of MFG_NAME). Re-recall rate = share of model-year + component combos recalled in 3+ separate campaigns; the denominator is combos recalled at least once. Listed the single combos with the most campaigns.
results.hit_means: A maker keeps recalling the same part on the same model year, so each fix didn't hold. The cleanest case is Freightliner Cascadia MY2019 service brakes: 13 campaigns from 2018-08 to 2023-10, plus 5 fatal complaints before the 2023 recalls.
results.miss_means: The Mercedes units lead is dead: it's rows repeating, not size. Once per campaign, Mercedes is 9.4M, behind Ford 94.3M, Chrysler 73.0M, GM 71.1M, Honda 62.1M and Toyota 61.6M.
results.boring: Tesla's 24% (81 of 338) comes from four models and software recalls under one component head, and it's widely covered. Subaru is 14.9%, Honda 13.3% (Takata waves), Hyundai 3.8%, Kia 2.9%. Altec's 21 campaigns on 'AERIAL DEVICE' MY2019 is a product category, not one model. The Ford E-350 repeats come from different upfitters.
traps: POTENTIALLY_AFFECTED_UNITS repeats on every line of a campaign. Take it once per CAMPNO.
Maker names drift: GM under 3 spellings, Chrysler under 3, Takata under 2.
NOTIFICATION_DATE uses 1111-11-11 as a placeholder, and 3,962 are null.

results.headline: E-bikes and mopeds (code 3215, split into 5045+5046 in 2024) went from 21.8K to 87.6K estimated ER visits, 2019 to 2023 (4.0x), while all injuries went 0.95x. Real, but CPSC publishes it. 2024-25 rises can't be trusted: weights reset in 2024 and floors jumped 1.22M in 2025.
results.checked: 9,794,971 rows 1999-2025. Summed STATISTICAL_WEIGHT by product code (any of 3 slots) and year, labels from the NEISS code book. Found codes that ended and their successors. Checked average weight by hospital stratum and year. Narrative fill by year. Who gets hurt (kids, sex, admitted) for the risers.
results.hit_means: E-bike and moped ER injuries quadrupled on a stable design while the total was flat. In 2025, e-bikes were 25% kids, 78% male, 14.9% admitted. UTVs went 3.0x (4.9K to 14.9K), but on thin samples (86 to 242 cases).
results.miss_means: Anything that only rises in 2024-2025 can't be told apart from the 2024 weight reset. Magnets, water beads, gummies and cannabis couldn't be tested, because the narrative is blank.
results.boring: CPSC publishes the micromobility rise itself. Not ruled out as 'already known'. Sample design is ruled in: the national total was +18% in 2024 on +7% cases, with average weight in stratum S 74.6 to 106.7 and V 16.9 to 27.6. Floors (1807) went 1.86M to 3.08M in 2025 in every stratum, which looks like a coding change.
traps: NARRATIVE is blank on all 3,924,911 rows 2015-2025. No text spot-check or keyword search is possible.
Weights reset in 2024: the national estimate rose 18% while sample cases rose 7%.
Floors (1807) +66% in 2025 across every stratum. That's most of 2025's +1.42M national rise.
Product codes split in 2020 (5042 to 5022/5025; 1329 to 5023/5024) and 2024 (3215 to 5045/5046). A new code looks like a new product with infinite growth.

results.headline: The 'most accident and fatality inspections' list is a California list. CA holds 30,245 of 60,050 type A and M inspections since 2015; Utah is next at 2,529. Inside CA: Sierra Pacific Industries 61, Foster Farms 47, Tesla 43 (18 still open, median 486 days to close).
results.checked: 5,196,412 inspections, one per ACTIVITY_NR. Inspection type mix; A (accident) + M (fatality/catastrophe, since 2011) since 2015 by state; top employers on normalized names, with sites, still-open cases and median days to close; split by 2015-19, 2020-21, 2022-26 and by CA. Inspections opened 2015-2020 with no close date, by employer.
results.hit_means: An employer keeps drawing accident inspections at many sites, measured against same-state peers. Sierra Pacific: 67% of its inspections are accident-type, at 16 sites. Tesla's cases stay open far longer than the others'.
results.miss_means: The national ranking says nothing: UPS 107, Walmart 54 and Safeway 53 are mostly CA counts. The open-case list is state bookkeeping: 9,809 of 464,524 from 2015-2020 are still open, led by Maryland contractors, a Puerto Rico name fragment 'DE', and test rows.
results.boring: California uses type A (26,721) where Texas, Florida and New York use M. Likely because Cal/OSHA investigates serious-injury reports too; this table can't prove it. Big employers have more sites. Kaiser's 24 of 36 fall in 2020-21 (COVID). There's no headcount denominator (NR_IN_ESTAB is junk). Not ruled out. Next step is the OSHA 300A join inside CA.
traps: 'TESTING OIS 2' test inspections: 21 rows across 20 states.
California's type A is not the same as other states' type M. Don't pool them nationally.
Still-open counts are driven by Maryland and Puerto Rico bookkeeping, not by employers.
Name drift splits UPS ('UPS'), Walmart ('Walmart Stores') and Amazon across several keys.

results.headline: The triage premise is backwards: the two big chains are at or below average (death rate DaVita 22.11, Fresenius 21.32, all clinics 21.80). The outliers are nursing-home dialysis operators (Dialyze Direct, Concerto, Home Dialysis Services). They run 46 clinics with a median of 1 chair, and 20 of them are rated Worse than Expected on survival (20 of the 38 with a rating), against 2.3% for everyone else. Their weighted death rate is 32.27 vs 21.65. The other independent for-profits still run 7.8% Worse than Expected, and 9 of Maryland's 12 Worse-than-Expected clinics are independent for-profits.
results.checked: Grouped all 7,557 clinics into DaVita, Fresenius, other chains and independents (for-profit and non-profit). Per group: patient-weighted death and hospital-stay rates, share rated Worse than Expected on survival, stars, and each clinic minus its own state's average. Then listed the independent for-profits rated Worse than Expected, and matched facility names for the nursing-home dialysis brands [Q7, Q8, Q22, Q23, Q29].
results.hit_means: A small, named set of multi-state operators has a death rate about 50% above everyone else's even after CMS adjusts for patient mix. The CCNs and names are in hand for a deeper pass.
results.miss_means: CMS's death-rate model already adjusts for nursing-home residence and a like-for-like check closes the gap. Then this is only the frailty of nursing-home patients.
results.boring: Nursing-home residents are the sickest dialysis patients. Not ruled out: I did not check whether the CMS death-rate model adjusts for nursing-home status, and that is the first thing to read. The chains-vs-independents angle is ruled out, since the two big chains sit at or below the average.
traps: CHAIN_ORGANIZATION = 'Independent' does not mean a single clinic. Dialyze Direct alone has 6+ CCNs in 5+ states under that label, and the brand name match also pulled clinics labeled DaVita, DCI and Other.
MORTALITY_RATE_FACILITY is a risk-adjusted rate per 100 patient-years (like 17.9), not a ratio centered on 1. Some clinics show 0.

results.headline: Both triage angles are null in the pool. Across 81 clean switches to for-profit, the median charity change is -0.03 pts, and total charity went up, from $322.0M to $373.5M a year. For FY2022 bad debt vs charity, the median at cost is 0.52 for for-profit and 0.53 for nonprofit. One buyer stands out: at 11 hospitals whose enrollment Prime Healthcare holds, charity fell from $58.1M to $31.4M a year, -1.49 pts net of the same-state trend. Hospitals of the other 58 buyers rose 0.53 pts. The only FY2022 hospital with bad debt at cost over $20M and over 5x its charity is also enrolled under Prime: St. Mary's Regional Medical Center, Reno ($22.7M vs $2.98M).
results.checked: (A) Latest FY2022 report per short-term hospital: bad debt vs charity by ownership type, both raw and with bad debt converted to cost via the cost-to-charge ratio. (B) TYPE_OF_CONTROL moving from nonprofit or government to proprietary between back-to-back years, stable for 2 years on each side (172 raw flips, 81 clean). Charity as a % of total costs, 2 years before vs 2 years after, netted against same-state hospitals that never changed type. Buyer taken from HOSPITAL_ENROLLMENTS by CCN [Q9, Q10, Q24-Q28, Q30].
results.hit_means: One named buyer's hospitals cut free care by about 46% after purchase, while other for-profit buyers' hospitals rose. That points at a buyer-specific practice.
results.miss_means: With only 11 hospitals, mostly in New Jersey where charity-care subsidy rules and Medicaid expansion moved things, the gap is noise plus policy.
results.boring: Charity follows Medicaid expansion, and bad debt is at charges while charity is at cost. The markup artifact is ruled out: the raw bad-debt-to-charity gap (3.72 vs 2.15) vanishes at cost. Expansion is netted out for the pool with a same-state trend, but only partly for Prime (n = 11; NJ's trend fell 0.36 to 3.07 pts over those years). Prime has had press coverage before.
traps: HOSPITAL_ENROLLMENTS names today's owner, not the buyer at the switch. MUSC Health Kershaw switches to for-profit in 2019 but is enrolled today under the Medical University Hospital Authority; the for-profit owner in between is in neither table.
TOTAL_BAD_DEBT_EXPENSE max of $20.4B is a typo: Sullivan County Community Hospital (151327), FY2016. Every other year's max is $0.25-1.03B. 2-10 reports a year show bad debt above total costs.
Bad debt is at charges and charity is at cost. Never divide one by the other raw.
1,090 reports share a CCN-year with another report, and 2,916 cover under 300 days. Sum within a CCN-year before comparing years.

results.headline: The table can name big sellers ahead of collapses: 987 of 22,770 owner-months with $5M+ sold came before a price at least 50% lower, 4-9 months later. Candidates include Daniel Loeb in Upstart ($712M at $225, later $51), Ernest Garcia II in Carvana ($329M at $353, later $105) and Artal Group in WW ($456M at $76, later $20). But the top of that list is stock splits (Tesla, Walmart, Alphabet). The 10b5-1 plan flag exists only in a 2026-Q1 table that doesn't overlap these trades, and the FDA-recall timing test was small ($78.2M sold before recalls vs $605.8M in the control windows).
results.checked: Sales only (code S), 2015-2026, price $0.01-10,000, value up to $10B. Summed per filing, then attached the issuer (submission table) and the first reporting owner, ranked by dollars. Searched both databases for the 10b5-1 checkbox column. Matched 25 issuers to FDA Class I recall firms on the full name and compared sales 30 days before each recall with the window 60-90 days before, same issuer. For owner-months with $5M+ sold, compared the sale price with the issuer's own median insider trade price 4-9 months later [Q1, Q2, Q11-Q14].
results.hit_means: A named candidate list of insiders who sold big blocks just ahead of a collapse, ready for checking against real price data and filings.
results.miss_means: Without the plan flag and a real price feed, every name can be explained as a scheduled plan, a lockup expiring, a secondary offering or the 2022 market-wide crash.
results.boring: 10b5-1 plans can't be ruled out: the AFF10B5ONE checkbox is only in FINANCE__FED_SEC_EDGAR_INSIDERS (filed Jan-Mar 2026), and this table has 2 rows from 2026. Lockup expiries at the 2021 top and the 2022 crash are not ruled out either. The recall angle is ruled out as small: without Walmart it is $76.7M before vs $46.2M in the control windows, mostly Pfizer.
traps: Joint filers repeat the same trades: Alice, Rob and Jim Walton show $24.63B each for the same trades.
Blank shell companies report $975-1,000-a-share 'sales' worth up to $19.5B each (owners James Cassidy and James McKillop), under the $10B-per-row cap.

A stock split looks like a crash in insider trade prices. A ratio-based split guard fails both ways: it flagged Unity and Snowflake, which did not split, and missed Tesla 3:1 and Walmart 3:1, which did.
Coverage is lopsided: 1.71M rows before 2022, about 290K a year for 2022-2024, 97,575 for 2025, and 2 for 2026.
Snowflake regex has no \b word boundary, so a name-normalizing regex that uses it silently does nothing.

results.headline: 706 of 8,234 FDA-regulated US phase 2-4 trials (8.6%) that finished between 2017-01-18 and 2022-06-30 have no results posted as of the 2026-09-04 snapshot, covering 152,850 enrolled patients. Industry misses 9.0%, academic 8.2%, NIH 2.0%. It is a long tail: 537 sponsors, 435 of them missing exactly one. The biggest holders are Brigham and Women's (9 of 35) and UC San Diego (9 of 26). Big pharma is at 0 (BMS 0 of 101, Gilead 0 of 86).
results.checked: Interventional trials with PHASE holding phase 2, 3 or 4 (1/2 included), a US site in LOCATIONS, status completed or terminated, and primary completion between 2017-01-18 and 2022-06-30, so the 1-year deadline plus a 2-year delay has passed. Split by the FDA-regulated flag and sponsor class, then ranked sponsors by trials with HAS_RESULTS false, with and without a 20-trial floor [Q5, Q6, Q19-Q21].
results.hit_means: Named academic centers and small biotechs are sitting on finished, legally covered trials with thousands of patients enrolled.
results.miss_means: The missing results are a mix of 'submitted but stuck in NLM review', certified delays and defunct sponsors. The table can't separate these, and no sponsor holds more than 9.
results.boring: The FDAAA TrialsTracker already publishes sponsor league tables for exactly this, and the per-sponsor counts are small. Not ruled out. Not-regulated trials (59% missing) are excluded because the law doesn't bind them.
traps: RESULTS_FIRST_POSTED_DATE is the public posting date after NLM review, not the submission date the law counts. By it, 6,512 of 7,528 reporters look 'late', which is meaningless.
IS_FDA_REGULATED_DRUG and _DEVICE are blank on 223,743 rows (older records). 2,504 trials in the set have a blank flag, with a 10.0% no-results rate.
NPI is null on all 601,694 rows, as the traps file already says.

results.headline: Indivior paid only $170,922 in 2022 to 2,604 buprenorphine prescribers, and their Suboxone+Sublocade share barely moved (12.0% paid vs 11.1% not paid). The top 20 by maker money are Alkermes-paid psychiatrists and NPs ($41K-$134K, mostly speaker fees), with 0 Vivitrol claims for 15 of 20. The only lift is Vivitrol at 12.0% vs 5.8% among Alkermes-paid prescribers, on $2.77M of money: the known money-follows-prescribing pattern. Also, 37% of the table's $636.0M 'addiction' drug cost is pain drugs.
results.checked: Part D 2022 brand-by-generic totals behind the six generic names. Payment buckets (all-company TOTAL_PAYMENTS) within each prescriber type, comparing median addiction claims and cost. Open Payments 2022 money from Indivior, Alkermes, Orexo and BDSI/Collegium per NPI, against each prescriber's share of that maker's own brand in Part D 2022, paid vs not paid. Top 20 by maker money, with names checked against the addiction table [Q3, Q4, Q15-Q18].
results.hit_means: If makers' money bought brand share, paid prescribers would show clearly higher own-brand shares at meaningful dollars. Only Vivitrol (2x) and Belbuca (44.8% vs 30.8%) show a lift, both on small money.
results.miss_means: Indivior's money is meal-sized and moves nothing, and the top-paid are paid for other drugs. The story as pitched is not here.
results.boring: Volume and specialty drive both the money and the claims: paid prescribers have bigger panels (Indivior median 71 claims vs 37). Alkermes also sells antipsychotics, so its psychiatrist speaker fees are almost surely for those; the Open Payments mart has no product column to prove it. Confirmed rather than ruled out.
traps: The six 'addiction' generic names hide pain drugs: Belbuca $123.0M, generic 'Buprenorphine' $88.0M (most likely the pain patch at $330 a claim; mono tablets file as 'Buprenorphine Hcl' at $70), Butrans $13.9M, and Part D methadone $11.8M (pain; addiction methadone comes from clinics, not Part D). Together $236.7M, 37% of $636.0M.
TOTAL_PAYMENTS and TOP_MANUFACTURER are all companies and all drugs. The top payer is often AbbVie, Lilly or Novo, not an addiction-drug maker.
Part D hides drug rows under 11 claims, so a 0 brand claim means 'under 11 or none'.

results.headline: California's counselors and family therapists turned Medicare down at 2.3x the rate of its psychologists and social workers: 35.8% vs 15.6% opt-out share. 4,890 opted out; 199 billed 11+ Medicare patients in 2024. Nationally, 4.2 counselor/MFT opt-outs per 2024 biller, against 0.54 for psychologists and social workers. The triage premise was wrong: counselors didn't 'leave,' they declined to join when the benefit opened in January 2024.
results.checked: Opt-outs by specialty and start year. Counselor (MHC) and MFT opt-outs by month, July 2022 to 2026. By state: opt-outs next to PECOS billing enrollments (order-and-refer-only left out) and 2024 Part B billers with 11+ patients, for MHC+MFT, with psychologists + clinical social workers in the same state as peers. Opt-out share = opted out / (opted out + billing enrollments).
results.hit_means: Counselors and therapists refuse Medicare far more than their peers in the same state. The 2024 benefit has names on paper but few people seeing seniors: CA 24.6 opt-outs per biller, WA 17.7, OR 10.6.
results.miss_means: If the rates matched their peers, opting out would just be the normal cash-pay default, with no story specific to counselors.
results.boring: Not ruled out: first-year ramp. 2024 was the first billing year, and Part B hides billers with fewer than 11 patients, so 3,458 is a floor. Also not ruled out: CA and WA have large private-pay therapy markets, and low Medicare rates are the known cause. Ruled out: opt-out as a first step toward enrolling (only 1 NPI is on both the opt-out list and PECOS), and renewal double-counting (renewals are automatic and add no rows). 99.8% of MHC/MFT opt-outs started 2024 or later; 5,114 in January 2024 alone, down to about 150-210 a month by 2026.
traps: The opt-out file is a snapshot of who is opted out now: every OPTOUT_END_DATE is 2026-06-30 or later and the effective date is the FIRST opt-out, so counts by year mean 'still opted out, by start year.' Anyone who returned to Medicare has dropped out of the file.
PECOS PROVIDER_TYPE_DESC mixes billing enrollments with 'ORDER AND REFERRING ONLY' rows; filter to PRACTITIONER% before calling anyone in-network.
No 65+ population table was found for a seniors-per-counselor denominator, and the opt-out file has ZIP but no county.

results.headline: The top opioid and antipsychotic names are volume and specialty artifacts. 292 Part D 2024 prescribers are on the OIG ban list (283 with the last name agreeing), but 291 were banned in 2024 or later, and the one earlier ban (Eduardo Miranda, Laredo TX, 2015, $7.5M of 2024 drug cost) has HAS_WAIVER = True. Non-psychiatrists wrote 78% of antipsychotic claims for patients 65+ (11.1M of 14.2M), which is a known story.
results.checked: Long-acting opioid claims per NPI, ranked against the specialty's top 1% among prescribers with any long-acting claims (family practice cutoff: 231; Bruce Mackey, Edmond OK: 2,289, which is 9.9x). Antipsychotic claims for 65+ ranked by count, then by share of 65+ claims inside a band of 904 non-psych prescribers with 30,000+ claims for 65+ (median 2.08%, p99 7.03%). Every Part D NPI joined to LEIE on NPI with last name as the second field. All names are data matches, not verified against primary records.
results.hit_means: Named prescribers far above their peers who were also banned and still paid would be an enforcement-lag story. Four top-list names were banned after 2024: Nathan Hanflink (#60 on opioids, banned 2026 under 1128b7), Lawrence Peters (#217 on long-acting, 2025, 1128a4), Alexander Frank (#409 on antipsychotics, 2025, 1128a2), Randall Berinhout (2025, 1128a1).
results.miss_means: The top lists are pain practices and nursing-home volume: the well-worn prescriber-list story. The national #1 antipsychotic prescriber (Pearlstein, PA) has 351,254 claims for 65+, and his 4.9% share sits at about the band's 90th percentile.
results.boring: Ruled in: pain practices filed as family or internal medicine (Mackey's opioids are 79% of his claims); nursing-home doctors carry huge volumes; psych-heavy patient panels in PR, Miami and Chicago. Ruled out: rates of 100 on small denominators (ranked on counts and in-band shares, not OPIOID_PRSCRBR_RATE) and suppression junk (antipsychotic flag only '*' or blank, no non-numeric values). 'Banned later' is about 10x the base rate among the top 1,000 long-acting prescribers, but that's only 2 people.
traps: Antipsychotic absolute ranks are volume: rank on share within a volume band, not on the raw count.
LEIE HAS_WAIVER is load-bearing: a banned prescriber with a waiver can legally be paid. Check it before calling a banned-and-paid hit.

results.headline: The exclusion angle is dead: $100,322 went to 14 payee lines barred before payment with the city agreeing, and $12.5M in all city-agreed ban matches, out of $135.06B. Relief tracked revenue: short-term hospitals got 7.0% to 8.8% of 2019 net patient revenue across Medicaid quintiles. One lead: Beaver Valley Hospital (Beaver UT, 25 beds) took $22.3M, 2.45x its 2019 revenue, with 40 SNF enrollments under its name.
results.checked: Payee NAME_KEY + state against LEIE (all rows) and SAM (all agencies but HHS), with city as the second field and the ban date compared with 2020-04-10. Payee key + city + state against FY2019 HCRIS: 1,501 hospitals matched of 6,036 reports, 780 usable short-term hospitals, $20.7B. Measured paid / 2019 net patient revenue and $/bed by Medicaid-day quintile. For outliers, counted SNF enrollments under the hospital's own name.
results.hit_means: Barred providers cashing big checks, or rich hospitals paid more per bed or per revenue dollar, would be the story.
results.miss_means: Tiny hits and flat ratios mean the formula worked as written, which is what showed up. The median $/bed is flat at $115K-$125K, and the most-Medicaid quintile got slightly more per revenue dollar (8.2% vs 7.0%).
results.boring: Ruled in: the revenue formula (flat ratios) and name collisions. For LEIE persons barred before payment, the city differs on 220 of 228. Critical-access hospitals got a median 19.8% of revenue against 8.2% for short-term hospitals: the rural tranche by design. Of the 52 hospitals paid more than 50% of revenue, 33 are critical-access and only 5 have nursing homes under the same name. Match bias: systems paid under a system name miss.
traps: A relief-fund hospital payee can carry nursing-home money: Beaver Valley Hospital (UT) has 40 SNF enrollments under its name and took 2.45x its 2019 revenue.
A later ban is not a ban at payment time: 47 organization lines ($11.2M) were banned after taking the money (e.g., Maison De'Ville Nursing Home, Houma LA, $1.09M, banned 2022).

results.headline: LVADs top the death reports by design: HeartMate 3 1,748 and HVAD 1,242, in a product code where 12.6% of reports are deaths. The one sharp outlier is Nevro's Senza spinal stimulator: 168 death reports on 737 total (22.8%), against 76 on ~42,200 (0.18%) for the rest of its code. None of the 168 flag a device problem, which points at reporting practice. Dexcom has only 7 death reports, so the Dexcom angle is malfunction volume, not deaths.
results.checked: Death and injury reports (distinct MDR_REPORT_KEY) by maker x product code, compared with all makers in the same product code. For outliers: PRODUCT_PROBLEM_FLAG, event-date age, and reports per receive day. Injuries by brand: peak month against median month.
results.hit_means: A maker with far more deaths than its own product-code peers, with device problems flagged and spread over time, would point at device-specific harm.
results.miss_means: The death share tracks the product code. That's volume and sick patients.
results.boring: Ruled in: LVAD patients die of heart failure. Spectranetics Stellarex has 147 of 158 death events before 2020: retrospective paclitaxel trial reports, known since 2019. HVAD batch-filed 98 death reports on 2021-08-20 after sales stopped. Essure's 18,838 injuries (peak April 2020, 5x its median month) are litigation-driven. Only 21 months are loaded (2020-01 to 2021-09). Open: Nevro under-reports everything but deaths, or its peers skip deaths. Spinal stimulators were widely covered in 2023.
traps: MAUDE death reports aren't dated deaths: 3,131 of 15,013 death rows describe events before 2020, and batch days happen (HVAD 98 on one day).
PRODUCT_PROBLEM_FLAG is 'N' on most death reports (Nevro 0 'Y' of 168), so a death report doesn't mean the device failed.

results.headline: 478 Class I recall events are still Ongoing (1,735 product rows, 199 firms). 64 have been open longer than the 4.6 years that 90% of closed Class I recalls took (median close: 733 days). 14 of the 64 are the HeartWare/Medtronic HVAD pump, which is still implanted in patients. Medline leads on ongoing Class I events (25) once its two name spellings are merged.
results.checked: Class I recalls with status Ongoing, counted as distinct EVENT_ID per firm, with the oldest start and days open up to the newest REPORT_DATE (2026-07-29). Yardstick: days from start to termination for 473 Class I events closed since 2012 (median 733, p90 1,682). Listed every open event past the p90.
results.hit_means: Firms whose 'can kill' recalls stay open far longer than their peers': the fix never reached the devices. Candidates: Philips Trilogy foam (2018, 8.1 years, 229,353 devices), Allergan textured implants (2019, 4.0M units), MiniMed 630G (2019), BD Alaris (5 events, plus 3 repair shops).
results.miss_means: Open times fall inside the normal closing range. Nothing there.
results.boring: Ruled in: implanted devices (HVAD, pacemakers, breast implants) keep a recall 'ongoing' while patients carry them, and FDA closes the paperwork slowly. Kit assemblers like Medline multiply rows. Philips and HVAD are famous. Sensitive: 36 of the 64 started in 2021, right at the cutoff.
traps: RECALLING_FIRM isn't normalized: Medline appears under 2 spellings (13 + 12 events), HeartWare under 5. Counting by firm splits one company.

RECALL_INITIATION_DATE can be retrospective: Abiomed event 98868 started 2011-01-17 and was classified 2026-05-28 ('Retrospective submission'). Check CENTER_CLASSIFICATION_DATE before quoting a recall's age. One Class II row starts in 1930.

results.headline: SpaceX, Ford and Bath Iron Works still ran 2.5-3x their industry peers' injury rates in 2025 (3.12x, 2.47x, 2.67x; in 2024 they were 3.27x, 2.14x, 3.01x). Electric Boat (0.81x) and Ingalls (1.10x) stayed normal. This updates F-035 to F-037; it is not a new find. The deaths and top-rate angles are dead.
results.checked: Tagged SpaceX, Ford, Bath, Electric Boat and Ingalls sites by name in 2024 and 2025. Kept sites logging 500-4,500 hours per worker. Rate = recordable cases per 200,000 hours (per 100 full-time workers). Peer = all other sites in the same 6-digit NAICS that year with the company removed, falling back to 4-digit when peers log under 5M hours. Separately: ranked 2025 deaths by site and company, matched death sites to 2024 on ESTABLISHMENT_ID with ZIP agreement, and ranked 4,368 sites with 500+ workers by rate vs peers.
results.hit_means: The injury gap held a third year: still about 3x after the 2023 Reuters story. Bath is clean: one site, 6,638 workers, 11.82 vs 4.42 at other shipyards.
results.miss_means: If the ratios had dropped toward 1x, the 2023-24 findings would be a blip. They didn't.
results.boring: Not fully ruled out. The SpaceX name tag pulls in contractors (ABM janitorial, PCAM valet, Performance Contractors) worth 39 of 478 cases and about 5.1M of 50M hours. SpaceX's own 10 sites (EIN 010627671) are 439 cases on about 44.9M hours = 1.96; the own-site peer ratio still needs a rerun. Ford's 2025 filing adds office and engineering sites (52 to 80 sites), so it needs a plants-only rerun. Thin 6-digit pools (481212) fall back to 4-digit. The deaths list is known disasters (Accurate Energetic Systems 16, UPS airline 3, U.S. Steel Clairton 2) plus typos. The top-rate list is NAICS miscodes.
traps: 193 column-shifted rows (STATE not two letters, or COMPANY_NAME all digits) carry 18 deaths, including a fake 16-death row ('Grand Prairie', company '332321')
Deaths typed with zero cases: Rosen Inn hotel 10 deaths / 0 cases; Capriati Construction 6 / 0
NAICS miscodes top any worst-rate list: hospital filed as 524114 insurance, Wegmans store as 551114 HQ; Cleveland Clinic Beachwood shows 2,192 cases for 541 workers
The 'half-loaded 2025' trap is stale: 383,283 rows = 96% of 2024's 398,620; filings stop 2026-03-15, so only the late filers are missing
Name tags catch contractors at the named company's sites; tag by EIN instead

results.headline: 13,037 tails (4.1%) and 4,319 of 29,000 jets (14.9%) sit with owner-trustees. The sanctions join found 0 confirmed hits. One lead: Aircraft Guaranty Corp Trustee (Oklahoma City) still holds 364 valid, unexpired tails and added 38 new certificates in 2024-26 (6, 18, 14) after 1 in 2021-23. Press reports tie the company to its owner's 2023 cartel-aircraft conviction; that is not verified and no warehouse list names it.
results.checked: Counted TYPE_REGISTRANT codes and TRUSTEE-named owners, and ranked trustee names and addresses by tails and jets. Joined N-numbers to tail numbers pulled from OFAC SDN remarks and OpenSanctions airplane records. Exact-matched multi-word company registrant names to OFAC SDN, current SAM entity exclusions and OpenSanctions, then checked city or state. Looked at Aircraft Guaranty and Southern Aircraft Consultancy by status and certificate year, and searched every warehouse list for Aircraft Guaranty and its owner.
results.hit_means: A trust company tied to a drug-plane conviction kept taking on new US registrations after the verdict. That is worth an outside check of court and FAA records.
results.miss_means: Tail join: 0 of 1 OFAC N-tail and 0 of 344 OpenSanctions planes are on today's registry. Name join: 0 OFAC hits, and all 3 SAM hits fail the city check (Burleson vs Parkland, Covington vs Chillicothe, Wilmington vs Grimes). Nothing sanctioned is visible, and name matching can't see through a trust anyway.
results.boring: Confirmed for the big trustees: Bank of Utah 1,844, TVPX/NetJets 1,419, Wilmington Trust 623 and UMB 574 are the legal norm for leased and foreign-owned jets, and the Boston Globe covered them in 2019. For Aircraft Guaranty, not ruled out: new owners may run it, or the FAA may already have reviewed it. Southern Aircraft Consultancy re-issued 511 of 514 certificates in 2026 at a shared Casper, WY agent address, which looks like an address move.
traps: No trust owner code exists: trustees file as corporation (3), LLC (7) or co-owner (4); search REGISTRANT_NAME for TRUSTEE
OpenSanctions rows with SANCTIONS filled include US bank enforcement orders (OCC/FDIC formal agreements) and export-control settlements (Lockheed, Honeywell, FedEx), which are not sanctions
STATUS_CODE mixes letters and numbers (V, W, 2-29); V = valid

results.headline: The 'quiet edits' are mostly churn: 163,012 of 173,284 fingerprint changes (94.1%) moved 50 bytes or less, and big changes hit every page on the same days. One real edit: 11 court-record pages whose address carried a plaintiff or party name (Giuffre v. Maxwell, Farmer v. Indyke x2, Bryant/Helm/Davies v. Indyke, Edwards v. Maxwell, L.M./M.J./C.L. v. Epstein, V.E. v. Nine East 71st) were renamed to name-free twins between Feb 22 and Feb 25, 2026. The old addresses answered 404 on Mar 5.
results.checked: Counted URLs, fingerprints and status codes. Grouped URLs by path. For each URL, ordered snapshots by time and flagged fingerprint changes by week with the size change and A-B-A flip-backs. Listed every non-200 answer and whether a 200 came after. Listed every court-records address with first and last snapshot and the answers seen.
results.hit_means: DOJ changed specific pages on a known date, and only the ones naming a survivor or party. That is small and specific.
results.miss_means: Everything else is template churn, bulk-crawl volume (from March, 85K-157K snapshots a week) and crawler blocks (401/403, back to 200 on almost every URL). The table holds 0 PDFs, so it can't show documents being pulled.
results.boring: Likely: a privacy scrub. Only 2 of the 11 named addresses (Bryant, Edwards) were saved live (200 on 2026-02-22); the other 9 were only seen as 403 or 404. The pages are listing pages about 12.5K in size, not documents, and 96% of snapshots are data-set 9/10/11 page lists.
traps: No documents in this table: 0 PDF rows; every row is an HTML listing page (the 18.1K max is the main disclosures page)
94% of fingerprint changes are 50-byte churn; big changes land site-wide on the same day (01-17, 01-30, 03-04, 03-18/19, 05-09/10)
404s are mostly junk URLs (%0A, %5C) and guessed data sets 24-39 that never existed
Snapshot volume is a crawl artifact: hundreds a week before March, then 85K-157K a week

results.headline: FY2024 NIH overhead = $9.68B on $26.90B direct (36.0 cents per dollar). The peer median among 69 orgs with $100M+ direct is 38.0 cents. Top rates: Sloan-Kettering 57.6, Scripps 49.4, Boston Children's 48.4. Top dollars: Johns Hopkins $239.8M, UCSF $219.5M, Penn $208.9M. A 15% cap would cut about $5.65B, $140.7M of it at Hopkins. That is real but already published. Parked: the overhead share rose to 37.6% in FY25 and 40.0% in FY26 (partial).
results.checked: Summed INDIRECT_COST_AMT / DIRECT_COST_AMT by ORG_NAME for FY2024, NIH agency, parent rows only (11,010 subproject rows worth $4.43B left out), on rows with both costs. Ranked by overhead dollars and by rate within the $100M+ direct peer group. Computed loss at 15% of total direct. Ran the trend FY2019-2026 and by funding mechanism for FY24-26.
results.hit_means: The list of who loses most under a cap, with dollars and rate side by side.
results.miss_means: Nothing new against the February 2025 coverage. The same schools and institutes lead.
results.boring: Confirmed. Negotiated rates are public, the cap fight was covered nationally, independent institutes and hospitals are known to run highest, and F-008 already used this table. The cap math uses total direct, not the modified base the real cap used, so the losses are rough.
traps: Subproject rows (380,148 overall; FY2024 11,010 worth $4.43B) repeat money inside multi-project parents; sum parent rows only (per RePORTER docs, not checked row by row)
4,489 FY2024 NIH parent rows ($7.60B) have no overhead split; VA rows (2,181) have no award amount; ALLCDC rows have no cost split
