results.headline: 231 LA County hospices sit 3 or more to a street address (59 addresses), and all 231 are still on Medicare's certified list in a 2026 file. LA holds 16% of every US hospice enrollment (981 of 6,066). New lead: 12 hospices named 'CFHC NO4' through 'CFHC NO22, INC.' in San Antonio. 8 were incorporated on 2021-10-07, 6 share one building, and each has its own ASSOCIATE_ID. Data match, not verified.
results.checked: Grouped all 6,066 enrollments by street address (line 1 plus ZIP5) and compared metro areas by ZIP3. LA is ZIP3 900-918 plus 935. Two shares per area: incorporated 2019 or later (denominator: rows with a date) and at a shared address (denominator: all enrollments). LA: 56.1% incorporated 2019+ (rest of US 21.8%, CA outside LA/SD 34.2%) and 44.1% at a shared address (rest of US 3.9%). Peers: Houston 53%/32%, Las Vegas 66%/37%, Phoenix 54%/20%, Dallas 32%/26%, Chicago 33%/0%. Joined the stacked LA hospices by CCN to the certified list: 231 of 231 match, 206 certified 2019+. Listed the top addresses. 14545 Friar St, Van Nuys has 9 hospices, all incorporated Mar 2019 to Feb 2021. 7630 Vineland Ave, Sun Valley has 5, incorporated within 4 weeks in 2020. Pulled every CFHC-named row.
results.hit_means: Many new for-profit hospices share one building and one founding window. That is the hospice-mill pattern, and it is still in Medicare's 2026 roster. The San Antonio CFHC numbered series looks like one operator Medicare's own key does not tie together.
results.miss_means: If stacking were near the national 4%, it would be ordinary office clustering. It is 44% in LA.
results.boring: Partly ruled out. Office buildings do hold many small businesses. No two LA hospices share an exact suite (0), so this is same building, different suites. LA hospice fraud is already reported: LA Times, ProPublica, CMS enhanced oversight of new hospices in CA, NV, AZ and TX. The new parts are that it persists in a 2026 file and the San Antonio CFHC series. The facts.tsv claim of 'one NPI behind 45 enrollments' is false: max is 2 per NPI.
traps: facts.tsv says NPIs 1013548734, 1447931134 and 1487748646 each hold 45 rows. In the mart they hold 1 row each, and no NPI holds more than 2.
Same address means same building, not same suite: LA has 0 exact-suite matches.
No hospice owner table in the warehouse, so the people behind these companies are not reachable here.
ZIP3 is only a stand-in for county lines.

results.headline: 379 federal judges were assigned 3,650 cases naming a bank they owed money to that year (2003-2021). BofA 1,424, Chase 925, Wells 664. Most are ordinary cards and mortgages, which the recusal law does not treat as disqualifying. The narrow thread: 68 district judges with unusual loans from the bank (investment or rental property mortgages, guaranties, $250K+) on 424 cases naming it.
results.checked: Matched 17 big creditors by name in 18,775 debt lines. 961 judges owed one of them in some year (6,210 judge-bank-year pairs). Pulled only those judges' dockets and counted cases naming the same bank as a party, filed in the disclosure year or the next, with the judge still assigned. Split by debt type and suit type: 2,204 cases where the judge held a card with that bank, 791 a home loan. 899 foreclosure suits, 192 of them where the judge's home loan was with the same bank. Reran on 6 banks: 3,504 cases, 351 judges. 1,198 cases and 92 judges are in bankruptcy courts. Unusual loans: 716 cases and 90 judges, of which 424 cases and 68 judges are in district courts. Eye check: 12 of 12 random district hits had the bank as both party and creditor.
results.hit_means: The judge owed that bank money and stayed assigned to a case naming it. It only matters when the loan is unusual, or when the judge could sit inside a class, like a mortgage-terms class action against the judge's own lender.
results.miss_means: The creditor is never sued by that name (Amex, local banks), or the OCR broke the name. A miss proves nothing.
results.boring: Mostly stands. Suits against BofA/Countrywide, Chase and Wells filled every district in 2008-15, and cases are assigned at random. Under 28 USC 455, 'financial interest' means owning part of the party; an ordinary loan is not ownership. So unlike F-001's stock, most hits are routine. It also repeats probe 95 (2026-09-05: 831 cases, 150 judges, narrower key).
traps: VALUE_CODE is -1 on 2,728 rows and null on 1,674.
A third of bank-party hits (1,198 of 3,504) are in bankruptcy courts, where banks are in almost every case.
DATE_CREATED 2021-23 is CourtListener's own date. Use FINANCIAL_DISCLOSURES.YEAR_COL for the filing year.
Creditor names are OCR text ('AMCRICAN EXPRESS'); exact-name keys undercount.

results.headline: 2024: 47,607 doctor meals at exactly $125.00 and 20,666 at $124.99, against 675 at $126.00 and 192 at $123.99. $125 is a company meal limit, not a law: 28.6% of companies use it in one survey. AbbVie ranks 156th of 502 makers on bunching; it only leads on count. The real spread is between companies of the same size: AstraZeneca 11.1 meals per 1,000 just under $125, Pfizer 0.6.
results.checked: Counted raw 2024 Open Payments food-and-drink payments (14.1M) by band and by exact price. $100-124.99: 460,953. $125.01-149.99: 248,521. Over $125: 424,896 (3.0% of meals). Other spikes: $150.00 12,172, $100.00 4,430. From the mart, by year: the $124.00-124.99 band beats $125.01-126.00 by 5.2x, 4.9x and 4.4x (2022-24). Ranked 502 makers with 3,000+ meals over 2022-24 by meals in the $124.00-124.99 band per 1,000. The median maker has 2.91. Top: Dompé 33.2, Bausch & Lomb 25.4 (184K meals), Horizon 23.0, Phathom 19.4. AstraZeneca 11.1 (rank 37), AbbVie 5.0 (156), Novo 4.3 (190), Pfizer 0.6 (409). Web check on what the $125 line is.
results.hit_means: A maker prices meals at its own policy line. Exact $125.00 entries could also mean the reported value is the cap, not the real bill, which would be under-reporting. The data cannot tell a set-price $125 menu from a capped entry.
results.miss_means: A smooth price curve, with no policy line.
results.boring: Stands. The Sunshine Act has no $125 reporting line (the floor is about $13.82). $125 is a common company per-head cap. Big makers top the raw count because of sales-force size. The triage premise that AbbVie leads is rejected.
traps: The catalog and the dbt model call $125 a 'reporting cap'. It is a company policy cap.
The mart's N_JUST_ABOVE band (125.01-126.00) leaves out exactly $125.00, the biggest spike, so CLIFF_RATIO understates the pile-up.
AbbVie appears under two maker names (ABBVIE INC. and AbbVie Inc.).

results.headline: Judges with pension or payout deals from old law firms: 171 judge-firm pairs across about 160 firms. Only 26 pairs, on 42 published opinions, show that firm as counsel before the judge in the agreement years, and many of those are surname collisions. Most deals are fixed pensions with 'no control'.
results.checked: Classified 10,007 lines: 2,517 law-firm-like, 3,962 government or public plans, 3,528 other, 608 with payout words. Found firm names; no firm is tied to more than about 3 judges. Matched about 160 firm name patterns to judges, giving 171 pairs (164 judges). Searched the ATTORNEYS text of 10.1M published opinions: 147,098 name one of those firms. Kept opinions where the docket's assigned judge is that judge or the JUDGES text names them. Result: 66 pairs and 356 opinions any year; 26 pairs and 42 opinions within disclosure years -2 to +1. Eyeballed the top 40.
results.hit_means: The judge was being paid through the firm's plan while the firm argued before them. Real-looking examples: Ikuta with O'Melveny (5 en banc opinions in Sarei v. Rio Tinto, 2010), and bankruptcy judges Chapman with Willkie, Mullin with Haynes and Boone, Taddonio with Reed Smith, matched by docket ID.
results.miss_means: Nothing. The warehouse has no docket-level attorney data, only the ATTORNEYS field on published opinions (mostly Harvard CAP, through 2018).
results.boring: Stands. Most firm agreements are fixed or closed pension plans and 401(k)s with 'no control', so the money does not ride on the firm's wins. The count is also small. Many hits are surname collisions: Andrew vs James M. Peck, Broderick in a New Hampshire state court, a different Roberts in D.D.C., William vs Robert Wilkins.
traps: Opinion-cluster JUDGES text collides on surnames. Use DOCKETS.ASSIGNED_TO_ID, or check the court.
PARTIES_AND_TERMS is OCR text with typos ('Bames & Thornburg', 'Retum of Capital').
FINANCIAL_DISCLOSURES rows are scrambled on many IDs; dedupe by ID before joining.

results.headline: The worst nursing-home chains did not take the most Covid relief. Per matched bed, chains under 2.5 stars got $8,193 and 3.5-star-plus chains got $10,692. The highest-fines quartile got $7,991 and the lowest got $9,129. The 'top relief per bed' decile is really a name-match-rate decile: 56% of its homes matched against 6% for the rest.
results.checked: On all 617 chains ($939.2M matched), compared the top 10% by relief per bed with the rest on stars, fines per bed and abuse-icon share. Then re-cut by star band and by fines-per-bed quartile. Per matched bed = matched dollars ÷ (matched homes × chain average beds per home), with and without parent-cheque matches. Listed the top 15 chains by dollars and their match method.
results.hit_means: If worse chains had taken more per bed, relief would have flowed toward the worst operators.
results.miss_means: What we got: worse chains took about 12-23% less per matched bed, and the top-relief decile is better-rated (3.12 vs 2.85 stars, $234 vs $342 fines per bed).
results.boring: Stands. Nursing-home relief was paid by formula (per facility, per bed) plus incentive payments tied to infection and death rates, which would favor better homes. $0 means no name match: 68% of the highest-fines chains show $0 against 55% of the cleanest. Chain quality is already covered by F-021 and F-029.
traps: Relief per total bed ranks name-match rate, not money. Divide by matched beds.
Per-matched-bed uses the chain's average beds per home, not the matched homes' actual beds.
ArchCare's $13.1M includes $7.1M of 'contains' name matches at 347 beds per home. Check before quoting.

results.headline: Outside groups of bankruptcy lawyers and advisers paid for 41.0% of bankruptcy judges' trips in 2011-19 (2,525 of 6,166), against 0.7% for district and appeals judges. Delaware's Kevin Carey reported 200 trips, 22.2 a year against 3.16 for other bankruptcy judges, 25 of them paid by the Turnaround Management Association. No sponsor is tied to a case.
results.checked: Joined reimbursements to disclosures to judges: 30,029 of 33,472 rows (89.7%) reach a judge. Disclosure years run 2003-2020, not 2021-23. Counted trips per judge, and who paid, split by bankruptcy, district and appeals judges (court from POSITIONS). Listed the law firms and companies that paid judges. Ran the docket test on Wolfson's personal-vacation sponsor (JSM at Falcon LLC, the Morrises): she is the assigned judge on 0 of 15 D.N.J. dockets naming JSM or Edgewood entities. Compared judges at the mega-case courts (Delaware, S.D.N.Y., S.D. Tex., N.J.) with other bankruptcy judges: as a group they are not more industry-funded (Isgur 18.4%, Jones 21.2%, peers 40.5%).
results.hit_means: The professionals who bill in bankruptcy cases help pay for the travel of the judges who approve their fees. One Delaware judge took 200 trips in nine years.
results.miss_means: Bar groups are never parties, so the 'sponsor later appeared before them' test can't run on about 97% of trips. The one personal sponsor tested came back clean. A docket shows only the last assigned judge, so a recusal looks like never being assigned.
results.boring: Speaking and teaching for ABI or TMA is permitted and routine, and the disclosures carry no dollar amounts. Not ruled out. Senechal's 75 trips paid by Robert Vogel Law Office are likely wind-down work from her former firm. Not checked.
traps: DATE_CREATED (2021-23) is the day CourtListener entered the row; the real disclosure year is FINANCIAL_DISCLOSURES.YEAR_COL, 2003-2020
Bankruptcy judges enter the collection only in 2011: bankruptcy-group trips run 2-8 a year before, 315-428 after
POSITIONS court list gives D.C. Circuit judges Ginsburg and Edwards the district court code 'dcd'

results.headline: Delaware holds 46 of the 80 Chapter 11 case families with $1B+ assets filed since 2015 (57.5%), against 3.2% of all families. But 'debt discharged' is not discharge ($196.8B on 4,257 still-pending cases), and 52 of Houston's 58 big families carry under $1M in assets. The dollar venue ranking is dead, and the count version is a known story.
results.checked: Kept one row per case (latest snapshot) for business Chapter 11 filings from 2015 on. Compared DEBT_DISCHARGED with TOTAL_DEBT by disposition and by pending flag. Grouped affiliate cases under their joint-administration lead, taking the largest asset figure per family, not the sum. Ranked districts by families with $1B+ assets, and separately by families with 20+ affiliate cases (Houston 58, Delaware 56, S.D.N.Y. 26), with a split by filing era.
results.hit_means: The mega-case concentration is real and measurable by family count: Delaware, Houston and S.D.N.Y. hold 140 of the 199 families with 20+ affiliates.
results.miss_means: Dollars can't rank venues, because Houston's assets are blank. 'Debt wiped out' can't be measured at all. The table has no debtor names.
results.boring: Venue shopping by Delaware, Houston and New Jersey is well covered. The six-snapshot double count was handled by keeping the latest snapshot. The 2.0T and 3.0T maxima weren't chased, because the dollar columns failed first.
traps: DEBT_DISCHARGED equals TOTAL_DEBT to the cent on 95% of filled closed cases and shows $196.8B on 4,257 still-pending, undisposed cases: it is scheduled debt, not discharged
TOTAL_ASSETS is under $1M on 52 of 58 S.D. Tex. families with 20+ affiliates; dollar venue rankings drop Houston
Snapshots start in FY2021, so pre-2020 filings that closed early are likely missing: 2-3 big families per district filed 2015-18 against 17-27 for 2019-22 (inferred)
The same-case key across snapshots is CASE_KEY; JOINT_ADMINISTRATION_LEAD's first 12 characters match CASE_KEY characters 3-14

results.headline: On real sanctions programs only: 0 FAA aircraft-owner hits and 13 contract-recipient name hits, with the country agreeing on 6. Those 6 got $7.5M in contracts, almost all before they were listed. The only money after a listing: NAI Logistics B.V., 13 DoD actions, net $20,647, dated within 3 days of its 2023-12-11 Global Magnitsky listing.
results.checked: The first pass on any non-empty SANCTIONS string returned junk: China's list aimed at US drone makers, OFAC and OCC settlements, Medicaid exclusions. The rerun kept only OFAC, EU, UK, UN, Canada, Australia, Swiss and Japan listings, with 2+ word company names and 3+ word person names, suffixes stripped and word order ignored. Matched against FAA registrants and USAspending R2 recipients (one row per name first), then checked the country and compared the list's FIRST_SEEN date with contract action dates. Also matched PPP borrowers: 7 hits, 6 collisions, and Sun Properties LLC ($157,400, KY) unresolved.

results.miss_means: No sanctioned company or 3+ word sanctioned person owns a US-registered aircraft under its own name. Nominee trusts would hide that, and this test can't see through them.

The LegalEntity type holds people's names from Medicaid exclusion lists
Filter on DATASETS by sanctions program; even '%Australia%Sanction%' pulls in Australia's list of banned skilled-visa sponsors
ECONOMICS__FED_SEC_EDGAR is only 200 rows, 20 CIKs, so it can't stand in for 'SEC filers'

results.headline: 2024 single-employer pensions hold 108.9% of what they owe in aggregate. 77 of the 1,583 plans owing $100M+ are under 80% funded, $67.1B short in all, and the big names are 79-94% funded. 631 plans report $426.7M in unpaid minimum contributions, but the 248 in real arrears have a median of 8 people. Two mid-size outliers: EIN 822871833, 25.8% funded with $95.4M unpaid, and Transit Management of Southeast Louisiana, $79.5M unpaid.
results.checked: Found one plan year (2024: 40,443 plans), not 17. Deduped 895 amendment double filings by EIN + plan number + year. Used SB_TOT_FNDNG_TGT_AMT, not triage's retirees-only column. Ranked shortfalls against the median $1B+ plan (104.6% funded). Named sponsors via the main Form 5500, IRS BMF and the PBGC plan list. Split unpaid minimums into arrears, timing and part-paid.
results.hit_means: Two mid-size plans carry $175M in unpaid contributions spanning several years. Both are worth a name lookup and a PBGC check.
results.miss_means: There's one year of data, so 'kept paying while the gap grew' can't be tested. The big-name shortfalls are ordinary. The biggest one (EIN 521893632, $4.70B) paid $990M against a $568.7M minimum.
results.boring: Big shortfalls sit at big old-industry plans that are already watched: confirmed. Unpaid amounts that equal this year's minimum (201 plans, $160.9M, including NTCA's $131.2M) point to filing before the contribution deadline.
traps: Schedule SB is one plan year (2024), not 17 years
895 plans were filed twice as amendments; dedupe by EIN + plan number + year, latest ACK_ID
SB_RTD_FNDNG_TGT_AMT is the retirees' slice only; the funding target is SB_TOT_FNDNG_TGT_AMT
Schedule SB doesn't join the main Form 5500 on ACK_ID: 0 of the top 25 matched
ECONOMICS__FED_PBGC_TRUSTEED_PENSION_PLANS holds live insured mega-plans (EIN 910425694, 298K participants), not failed plans
Unpaid minimum equal to this year's minimum usually means the filing came before the deadline, not arrears

results.headline: ACNR Holdings' underground coal mines logged 11.10 recordable injuries per 100 current workers a year in 2018-24. Other big coal owners ran 2.24-8.81, and Foresight ran 12.33. Marshall County Mine rose from 80 lost-time injuries (2018) to 150 (2025), steady across the Murray and ACNR owners. But ACNR's fracture and amputation rate (1.33) is middle of the pack: its lead is sprains and strains booked as days away.
results.checked: Confirmed injury code 01 matches IS_FATALITY (335 deaths in 2015-25). Capped each injury at 365 lost days. Rates are per 100 current workers from MSHA_MINES.NO_EMPLOYEES over 7 years, because there is no hours file. Compared each mine with peers of the same commodity and mine type (Marshall County 12.0 against a 2.7 median of 61 peers), and each owner with owners of 1,000+ workers. Split ACNR's years by who owned each mine at the time. Ran a severity test (fractures and amputations against sprains) and a total-recordables test against days-away share.
results.hit_means: ACNR and Foresight miners get hurt, or at least get recorded as hurt, at 1.5-3x the rate of other big coal owners, steady under two owners and rising at Marshall County.
results.miss_means: On serious injuries ACNR is ordinary, and part of its days-away lead is classification (87.8% booked as days away against 38.6-80.8% for peers). Deaths are too few (6-11 per owner) to rank.
results.boring: Today's headcount understates 2018-20 staffing at the post-bankruptcy owners, which inflates their rates. Not ruled out. More complete reporting looks like more harm. ACNR and Foresight already sit in F-010/B10 for violations. The fix is MSHA's quarterly employment and hours file, which isn't loaded.
traps: No MSHA hours or employment table exists in the warehouse; NO_EMPLOYEES is today's headcount only
Owners classify differently: ACNR books 87.8% of recordable injuries as days away, peers 38.6-80.8%; compare total recordables
A single injury can carry 3,616 DAYS_LOST; cap per injury before summing
Degree code 08 (natural causes) has 633 rows in 2015-25 and must stay out of harm counts; IS_FATALITY correctly equals code 01 only

checks.corrected_headline: 2,776 of 16,443 high-hazard dams are rated Poor or Unsatisfactory. On 634 of them the plan field says a flat "No", and on 119 more it says "Not Required". Measured against good dams in the same state, you'd expect about 453 without a plan, so the real extra is about 300. Most of it is in NC, NM, GA, SC, TX and MO. Drop Kentucky: 90 of its 91 say "Not Required", and so do 66 of its 79 good dams.
checks.reason:
VERDICT: NARROWED. The counts match exactly. The story on top of them does not hold as written.

**Reran it (Python door, read-only, 5 SELECTs)**
- Mart: 16,443 high-hazard dams, associated structures dropped. 2,776 rated Poor or Unsatisfactory, 2,776 distinct NID_IDs, so no duplicate loads. 753 have the plan flag False. One _SOURCE_RUN_ID. Same count in landing (16,443).
- BIA: 60 bad dams, 24 of them Unsatisfactory. Other spellings add nothing.

**What I found**

| # | Severity | Finding | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | blocker | **Kentucky "91 of 106" is a state-wide code, not bad dams missing plans.** 90 of the 91 say "Not Required" in the raw field; 1 says "No". Kentucky's good dams (Satisfactory or Fair) say "Not Required" on 66 of 79 and have a plan on only 15%, against 14% on its bad dams. | LIBRARY_RAW.LANDING.FED_NID_DAMS, EAP_PREPARED by condition, KY |
| 2 | real | **The flag merges three answers.** Staging sets `(upper(trim(EAP_PREPARED)) = 'YES') as has_emergency_action_plan`, so "No" and "Not Required" both become False. The 753 is 634 "No" + 119 "Not Required". The agent's no-NULLs check could never catch this, because it read the boolean, not the raw text. | C:/Code/Ripple_v6/library-onboarding/ripple_dbt/models/staging/fed_nid_dams/stg_fed_nid_dams__structures.sql (the has_emergency_action_plan line) |
| 3 | real | **The "about 95%" comparison uses Satisfactory dams only.** Satisfactory: 4,811 of 5,065 have a plan (95.0%). Fair: 4,191 of 5,113 (82.0%). The two together: 88.4%. Using each state's own good-dam rate, you'd expect 453 bad dams without a plan; there are 753. So about 40% of the 753 is just how each state reports. The bad dams are not the only ones missing plans. | Per-state good vs bad plan rates, landing |
| 4 | minor | **BIA is not part of the no-plan story.** It owns 60 bad dams, but only 4 of them have no plan. | Mart, OWNER_NAMES = 'BIA' |
| 5 | minor | **16.9% counts unrated dams in the denominator.** 3,489 high-hazard dams are unrated. Among rated dams the share is 21.4%, so 16.9% is a floor. | Mart |
| 6 | minor | **New Mexico's number is soft too.** Its 94 = 80 "No" + 14 "Not Required", and its good dams already lack a plan at 42%. Separately, 19 NM "No" rows carry a plan revision date, which contradicts the "No". | Landing, NM |
| 7 | minor | **May already be public.** AP counted poor high-hazard dams in 2019 (1,688). ASDSO, the state dam-safety officials' association, publishes plan coverage by state, as far as I know. I did not check either against primary sources. | Outside the warehouse |

**What survives**
- The 2,776 is real.
- The gap is real but smaller: bad dams lack a plan at 27.1% vs 11.6% for good dams nationally. After adjusting for state, the extra is about 300 dams, not 753.
- Extra no-plan dams over each state's baseline: NC +45, NM +33, GA +32, SC +30, TX +29, MO +19.
- Before any story: pull only the rows that say "No", and treat "Not Required" as a separate thread about state rules.

Every owner named here is a data match, not verified against primary records.

DISAGREE with the claim as written: Kentucky is a coding artifact; the comparison inflates the gap.

checks.corrected_headline: Lower Brule Sioux Tribe (data match, not verified) is the only one of 67,777 non-state auditees whose auditor flagged going-concern doubt and material noncompliance in all 10 years, 2016-2025. No other auditee has even 7 years of both. Its federal spending did double, $16.7M to $35.7M ($246.2M total), but so did the typical tribe's. The jump is 2021 COVID money, not money that grew because of bad audits.
checks.reason:
**Verdict: NARROWED.** The flag streak is real and rare. The "money kept growing" half is not about Lower Brule: every tribe's money grew.

**What I reran** (Python door, tag coverage-skeptic-2026-09-24; 8 statements: 4 SELECTs plus 4 session settings)

| Claim | Rerun | Status |
|---|---|---|
| One EIN, 10 years 2016-2025 | EIN 460222351, exactly 1 report per year, no duplicate loads | holds |
| Going concern 10/10 | Yes every year, no GSA_MIGRATION values | holds |
| Material noncompliance 10/10 | Yes every year | holds |
| $16.7M to $35.7M, $246.2M total | 16,657,266 to 35,668,193; the sum is 246.2M | holds |
| REDW since 2017 | Eide Bailly in 2016, REDW 2017-2025 | holds |
| 362 of 48,202 with going concern 3+ years | 362 of 48,202 | holds |
| Tribes: 13 of 827 | 16 of 898 when EINs that switch entity type are counted as tribal | minor: the definitions differ |

**Why it's rare (stronger than claimed)**
- Only 1 of 67,777 non-state EINs has both flags in 10 of 10 years. It's also the only one with both in 7+ years.
- Going concern 10/10 on its own: 5 auditees. Noncompliance 10/10 on its own: 79 (76 are local governments). The rare part is the pair.
- Tribal rates per report run 0.9-2.4% going concern and 5-9% noncompliance a year.

**Where it breaks: the money**

menu.verdict_on_existing: No lead from the coverage pass beats the best existing ones. All 10 new leads came back narrowed, several hard, and none tops the $593M alginate pair (F-032), the $96.8M skin-substitute surgeon (F-033) or the pill-to-death chart (F-002). The bottom of the old ledger is trivial next to the new finds: the null results (F-009, F-011 to F-018 and F-023) rank below every new lead and should come off the menu, while the 527 charity groups, the barred home-health owners and the CFHC hospices move into the upper-middle of the list.
